title: Module-Aware Optimization for Graph Neural Networks
authors: Guy Hadad, Haggai Roitman, Moshe Eliasof, Bracha Shapira
abstract: Different optimizers impose different geometries on parameter updates. Adaptive methods such as Adam and AdamW use coordinate-wise updates, while matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon utilize weight-matrix structure through orthogonalized updates. For Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), however, the effective geometry of its weight matrices is shaped not only by its learned channel-mixing weights, but also by the graph-propagated representations it acts on. Thus, even if an update is well normalized as a matrix, its effect on the layer output can be amplified when applied to graph-propagated features. To address this gap, we introduce GraphMuon, a graph-aware optimizer that adapts Muon's matrix updates to the covariance structure of graph-propagated layer inputs. GraphMuon performs orthogonalization in a metric defined by these propagated representations and normalizes step sizes according to the update's induced effect on the layer representation. We show that theoretically, vanilla Muon can suffer from graph-induced update amplification, while our GraphMuon can mitigate this effect. As such, our GraphMuon yields a graph-metric analogue of Muon's polar update step. Empirically, GraphMuon achieves $1.32\times$-$2.42\times$ validation-loss time-to-target speedups over AdamW on three large-scale OGB benchmarks. Across 15 dataset-architecture configurations spanning node classification, inductive graph classification, and graph regression, it achieves lower time-to-target in 13 cases, while maintaining competitive or superior predictive performance. Code is available at https://github.com/guy-hadad/GraphMuon.

infographic.key_insight: GraphMuon adapts matrix-aware optimization to graph-propagated feature geometry, mitigating update amplification that vanilla Muon can encounter in GNNs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: GraphMuon can reduce GNN training time to a target validation loss while maintaining competitive or superior predictive performance in the reported evaluations.
method: Model layer-input geometry using the covariance of graph-propagated representations.
Orthogonalize matrix updates in this graph-aware metric.
Normalize step sizes by the update’s induced effect on layer representations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 1.32×–2.42× validation-loss time-to-target speedups over AdamW on three large-scale OGB benchmarks and lower time-to-target in 13 of 15 dataset–architecture configurations.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify the overhead of covariance-aware updates, so assess memory and runtime costs on your target graphs and architectures.
infographic.paper_title: Module-Aware Optimization for Graph Neural Networks

title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
authors: Qile Jiang, George Em Karniadakis
abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.

infographic.key_insight: SwarmEvolve accelerates evolutionary program search using agent swarms that reason and exchange ideas in latent space rather than through lengthy text.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Latent-space collaboration could reduce search time and inference costs when optimizing programs for scientific computing and mathematical discovery.
method: Run hundreds of low-cost agents per round in swarms exploring different approaches.
Select distinct ideas using distances between agents’ hidden-state vectors.
Combine swarm members’ KV caches in a summarizer agent to enable latent-space crossover.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 21 problems, SwarmEvolve achieved the highest average score and matched scores reached by competing frameworks at 60 minutes in a median of 3–8 minutes.
infographic.watch_item: KV-cache sharing requires access to model internals, which may limit deployment through standard hosted LLM APIs.
infographic.paper_title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization

title: RM-VLM: From Natural-Language Task Descriptions to Vision-Grounded Reward Machines
authors: Roko Parac, Christos Ziakas, Leo Ardon, Alessandra Russo
abstract: Reward machines (RMs) have been proposed as a reward formulation in reinforcement learning (RL) to capture non-Markovian tasks where credit assignment depends on history. By representing reward functions as automata, RMs expose the task's temporal structure and allow such rewards to be handled within a Markovian framework. However, they assume a labelling function, a proposition-grounding oracle for observations, which must be manually engineered for each environment, limiting their wider applicability. In this work, we address this limitation by proposing RM-VLM, a novel approach in which a large language model (LLM) generates an RM from a natural-language task description, and a vision-language model (VLM) acts as the labelling function, grounding the RM's propositions over image-based observations during RM-guided policy learning. A VLM-based value function estimator is used to assess the agent's progress towards each RM transition and derive a dense reward signal. We evaluate RM-VLM on three domains covering non-Markovian grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection. Our experimental results show that RM-VLM consistently achieves higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods across all tested domains.

infographic.key_insight: RM-VLM combines language-generated reward machines with visual proposition grounding to guide reinforcement learning on tasks that depend on event history.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach reduces the need to hand-engineer environment-specific proposition labellers for visually observed, multi-step tasks.
method: An LLM converts a natural-language task description into a reward machine encoding temporal structure.
A VLM grounds the machine’s propositions in image observations during policy learning.
A VLM-based value estimator assesses progress toward reward-machine transitions to provide dense rewards.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across non-Markovian grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection, the abstract reports higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods, without numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Incorrect language-generated task logic or visual proposition grounding could produce misleading rewards and requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: RM-VLM: From Natural-Language Task Descriptions to Vision-Grounded Reward Machines

title: Unpacking the Compute Efficiency of Strong-to-Weak OPD against GRPO
authors: Zeyu Leo Liu, Yang Li, Bo Pang, Emre Can Acikgoz, Xuan-Phi Nguyen, Anurag Koul
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher's per-token supervision. Does this dense signal reduce the training FLOPs needed to reach a target accuracy compared with reinforcement learning? We systematically compare vanilla reverse-KL OPD with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) across task difficulty, student and teacher size, domain, and optimization choices, measuring held-out accuracy against training FLOPs. With an external post-trained teacher, OPD generally loses to GRPO in accuracy per training FLOP at matched settings, even when the teacher is further trained with GRPO, and often suffers response-length inflation. Yet a different teacher changes the picture: when the teacher is the student's own GRPO checkpoint, OPD recovers that checkpoint's accuracy on math with $50\times$ fewer distillation FLOPs than GRPO needs to reach the same accuracy. Following the same teacher setting, we consistently observe this high efficiency with a larger student, on code, and in a second model family. On a single domain, however, the GRPO checkpoint is already the desired model, so distilling it adds to total compute. Across domains, separate GRPO checkpoints hold different capabilities, and no single checkpoint serves every domain. Multi-teacher OPD (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) consolidates per-domain GRPO experts into a single student that matches each expert's accuracy, with the distillation stage costing only 5.2% (on 2 domains) and 8.0% (on 4 domains) of the specialist training FLOPs. Counting specialist training and distillation together, this pipeline reaches joint GRPO's performance on the 2-domain mix with 42.0% fewer total FLOPs.

infographic.key_insight: OPD generally trails GRPO in accuracy per training FLOP with external teachers, but efficiently recovers and consolidates capabilities from the student’s own GRPO-trained checkpoints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Training domain specialists with GRPO and consolidating them via multi-teacher OPD can reduce total compute compared with joint GRPO training.
method: Compare reverse-KL OPD with GRPO using held-out accuracy versus training FLOPs.
Vary task difficulty, model sizes, domains, optimization choices, and teacher source.
Distill domain-specific GRPO checkpoints into one student with multi-teacher OPD.
infographic.evidence_signal: Own-checkpoint OPD recovered math accuracy with 50× fewer distillation FLOPs; multi-teacher distillation cost 5.2% and 8.0% of specialist training FLOPs for two and four domains, respectively, while the two-domain pipeline matched joint GRPO with 42.0% fewer total FLOPs.
infographic.watch_item: The 50× result excludes teacher training: single-domain distillation adds total compute, and external-teacher OPD often inflates response length.
infographic.paper_title: Unpacking the Compute Efficiency of Strong-to-Weak OPD against GRPO

title: Data-driven discovery of intrinsic Lie point symmetries of differential equation systems
authors: Ilker Gurcan, Kadir Ustun, Ramazan Gokberk Cinbis
abstract: Discovering continuous symmetries directly from differential-equation data can reveal geometric structure for model reduction and scientific machine learning without symbolic determining equations or a closed-form representation of the governing system. We formulate intrinsic Lie point-symmetry discovery as an operator-theoretic problem on sampled jet-space data. Admissible generators are identified from a sampled determining operator and separated from redundant, solution-dependent, and geometrically trivial directions. The framework combines prolongation, sequential subspace restrictions, and a fixed nonlinear dictionary linear in trainable coefficients. A rank-stabilization preflight test diagnoses systems whose represented intrinsic symmetry algebra does not stabilize under dictionary refinement. On a controlled differential-equation benchmark with an analytically known 11-dimensional represented intrinsic symmetry algebra, the method recovers the complete represented generator set, reproduces its Lie-bracket structure to numerical precision, and approximates a known generator beyond the training domain. Here we show that explicit intrinsic continuous-symmetry generators can be recovered from data obtained from exact or approximate differential systems.

infographic.key_insight: Continuous Lie point-symmetry generators can be recovered directly from sampled differential-equation data without symbolic determining equations or closed-form governing models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Explicit symmetry generators can reveal geometric structure useful for model reduction and scientific machine learning.
method: Build a sampled determining operator on jet-space data using prolongation.
Apply sequential subspace restrictions to separate intrinsic generators from redundant, solution-dependent, and geometrically trivial directions.
Fit a fixed nonlinear dictionary linear in trainable coefficients, with a rank-stabilization preflight test under dictionary refinement.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a controlled benchmark, the method recovered all 11 represented intrinsic symmetry generators, reproduced their Lie brackets to numerical precision, and approximated a known generator beyond the training domain.
infographic.watch_item: Recovery is limited by the chosen dictionary; the preflight test flags cases where the represented symmetry algebra fails to stabilize under refinement.
infographic.paper_title: Data-driven discovery of intrinsic Lie point symmetries of differential equation systems

title: Conformal Prediction for Time-Dependent PDEs
authors: Joshua Stiller, Annika Schneider, Eyke Hüllermeier
abstract: Uncertainty quantification is crucial in scientific machine learning, where models inform safety-critical tasks such as flood forecasting, financial risk management, and thermal control in machines. Conformal prediction provides distribution-free coverage guarantees, but in time-dependent settings common to physics and engineering, these guarantees can break down, leading to systematic undercoverage. We study this problem in the context of surrogate models for time-dependent physical systems described by partial differential equations. We prove that in a function space setting, distributions at arbitrarily close times can be mutually singular, making exact coverage guarantees impossible. We further show that in discretized settings, the total variation distance between distributions often saturates exponentially fast with the grid resolution, mandating restrictions on the spatial discretization to ensure coverage. Finally, for certain settings, we show how to use principled weighted conformal prediction to obtain finite-sample coverage guarantees over growing time horizons.

infographic.key_insight: Conformal coverage can fail for time-dependent PDE surrogates because distributions at arbitrarily close times may be mutually singular.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable uncertainty bounds for applications such as flood forecasting and thermal control require accounting for temporal distribution shifts and spatial grid resolution.
method: Analyze temporal distribution shifts in function spaces.
Study total variation distance under spatial discretization.
Use weighted conformal prediction for growing time horizons in certain settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical results on mutual singularity, exponentially fast saturation of total variation with grid resolution, and finite-sample coverage in certain weighted-conformal settings; it specifies no empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Weighted-conformal guarantees are setting-dependent, and spatial discretization may need restrictions to preserve coverage.
infographic.paper_title: Conformal Prediction for Time-Dependent PDEs

title: How Far Can Untrained Neural Networks Go in Anomaly Detection? From Tables to Pixels
authors: Hyojun Yi, Geunyoung Kim, Hogeon Seo, Seunghyoung Ryu
abstract: Anomaly detection (AD) is often framed as a representation-learning problem, where strong performance is expected to require learned features or AD-specific optimization. However, this view can overlook the intrinsic separability of anomalies from normal references, even in the absence of learned representations. We therefore investigate how far untrained neural networks can go in anomaly detection. To this end, we propose PRISM, a framework combining fixed random nonlinear features with normal-reference Mahalanobis scoring for tabular detection and dense visual localization. Across 47 tabular datasets in ADBench, PRISM-T achieves the highest mean AUROC (86.4%) and the second-highest mean AUPRC (65.9%) among the compared methods. On MVTec AD and VisA, covering 27 visual categories, PRISM-V achieves mean image-level and pixel-level AUROCs of 90.4% and 96.4%, respectively. Notably, both models achieve these results without neural weight optimization or pretrained representations. A theoretical analysis further characterizes how nonlinear transformations affect the mean and covariance contributions to the Mahalanobis score gap, while empirical analyses examine the resulting score separability. These findings establish PRISM as both a competitive anomaly detector and a prior-to-learning baseline for assessing the added value of learned representations in anomaly detection.

infographic.key_insight: PRISM shows that fixed, untrained neural features can support competitive anomaly detection without pretrained representations or neural weight optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: PRISM provides a prior-to-learning baseline for testing whether representation training adds value in tabular detection and visual anomaly localization.
method: Generate fixed random nonlinear features.
Score anomalies using normal-reference Mahalanobis distances.
Use PRISM-T for tables and PRISM-V for dense visual localization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 47 ADBench datasets, PRISM-T achieved 86.4% mean AUROC (highest) and 65.9% mean AUPRC (second-highest); across 27 MVTec AD and VisA categories, PRISM-V achieved 90.4% image-level and 96.4% pixel-level mean AUROC.
infographic.watch_item: No neural training does not mean no fitting: Mahalanobis scoring still requires representative normal-reference statistics and numerically stable covariance estimation.
infographic.paper_title: How Far Can Untrained Neural Networks Go in Anomaly Detection? From Tables to Pixels

title: Adversarial Training with Large Step Sizes: Implicit Bias, Optimization, and Sharpness
authors: Yi Feng, Andrea Paudice
abstract: Adversarial Training (AT) is an important method for improving model robustness. We study the dynamics of deterministic Gradient Descent (GD) in AT. Most existing works in this direction focus on the small or vanishing step sizes regime, where GD resembles a continuous-time flow. However, such step sizes can make training inefficient and are rarely used in practice. In this paper, we study the AT dynamics of GD with large constant step sizes. We first study GD in adversarial linear logistic regression, focusing on two aspects: where the model parameters converge (implicit bias) and how quickly the losses decrease (optimization). We then turn to neural networks training and study how the sharpness of losses evolve during AT. Our results advance the understanding of the behaviors of GD with large step sizes in AT and highlight three key differences from its behavior in Standard Training (ST): (i) the implicit bias gap between AT and ST, previously established only for small step sizes, persists for arbitrarily large constant step sizes, (ii) different from ST, there is no uniform rate of convergence for the optimization error in AT, and (iii) sharpness can exhibit two-stage dynamics that differ from the Edge-of-Stability behavior observed in ST.

infographic.key_insight: With large constant gradient-descent step sizes, adversarial training differs from standard training in implicit bias, optimization convergence, and sharpness dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Large-step adversarial training may require distinct convergence expectations and sharpness monitoring rather than practices inherited from standard training.
method: Study deterministic gradient descent with large constant step sizes.
Analyze implicit bias and loss decrease in adversarial linear logistic regression.
Investigate loss-sharpness dynamics during adversarial neural-network training.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an implicit-bias gap for arbitrarily large constant step sizes, no uniform optimization-error convergence rate in adversarial training, and possible two-stage sharpness dynamics, but provides no datasets or numerical metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The analysis concerns deterministic gradient descent; applicability to stochastic optimizers and practical training pipelines is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Adversarial Training with Large Step Sizes: Implicit Bias, Optimization, and Sharpness

title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI
authors: Julian Kunkel, Ali Doosthosseini
abstract: Chat remains the default surface for many large language model (LLM) tasks, even as agentic tools such as OpenCode excel at coding and automation. Yet the model sees the current dialogue but not the workspace around it. We explore meta access---giving the assistant a structured, permissioned view of the interface itself and propose a ladder of levels: feature tutoring; metadata, settings, and preference access; retrieval over summaries and messages, confirmed mutation, and full orchestration. Meta access can turn a chat client from many screens into one entry point for finding, navigating, organising, and operating it, while raising risks around grounding, privacy, prompt injection, and trust. General-purpose agentic harnesses are runtimes; because they can change their own settings, meta access becomes reflexive and needs a separate control-plane boundary. We ground this in the Meta Chat prototype of the Chat AI client. It builds bounded context from, e.g., summaries, settings, and relevant messages; links references to conversations, topics, and personas; supports confirmed, reversible changes; offers a browsable tutorial library; and recommends personas as user-started conversations. By exposing application state in structured form, meta access can extend screen readers from widget descriptions to semantic workspace operations. Meta access thus turns chat from a window onto one conversation into a control layer for the whole workspace, extending chat toward agentic capability without surrendering user control. As assistants become embedded in IDEs, dashboards, office suites, and operating systems, AI-era interfaces should expose a structured, permissioned model of their state and capabilities, ideally by opening their existing metamodels through a debugger-like interface.

infographic.key_insight: Structured, permissioned access to application state can turn an LLM chat interface into a control layer for the whole workspace while preserving user control.
infographic.engineering_relevance: AI-enabled applications should expose structured state and capabilities, with a separate control-plane boundary for agents that can modify their own settings.
method: Define a meta-access ladder from feature tutoring and settings access to retrieval, confirmed changes, and full orchestration.
Build bounded context from summaries, settings, and relevant messages in the Meta Chat prototype.
Link workspace references and support confirmed, reversible changes, browsable tutorials, and user-started persona conversations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract grounds the proposal in the Meta Chat prototype for Chat AI but reports no quantitative evaluation or comparative results.
infographic.watch_item: Workspace access introduces privacy, prompt-injection, and grounding risks that require explicit permissions and clear control boundaries.
infographic.paper_title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI

title: A Generative Foundation Model for Multimodal Tokamak Tasks
authors: Yingshuai Ji, Haodong Feng, Guohong Deng, Gelin Bian, Yue Wang
abstract: Tokamak experiments record diverse measurements, including waveforms, profiles, fields, and scalars, which are used to reconstruct the plasma, forecast its evolution, recover associated control signals, and estimate disruption risk. Most models are built separately for one task and a fixed set of inputs and outputs, and each relies on a prescribed subset of diagnostics rather than structuring the full multimodal observation set to extract global, cross-signal information about the discharge. These limitations motivate a reusable foundation model that adapts to each task's input-output schema and models heterogeneous target signals jointly, rather than retraining a separate model for every configuration. In this work, we extend the TokaMark benchmark with two groups of tasks for actuator action inversion and disruption prediction, yielding 20 MAST tasks in six groups with explicit schemas and evaluation protocols. Then, we introduce GenToka, a generative tokamak foundation model that jointly generates schema-selected targets through a shared conditional diffusion Transformer, with signal-specific codecs preserving native time series, profiles, fields, and scalars; foundation pretraining and task-specific adaptation transfer cross-signal structure across all six groups. Evaluation on MAST measurements shows that GenToka reduces macro-average normalized root mean squared error relative to TokaMind by 4.7% on Groups 1-4 and by 17.7% on Group 5, and improves macro-average window-level F1 on Group 6 by 8.4% at a common validation-selected threshold. GenToka provides a reusable, generative, and multimodal pathway for experimental tokamaks, linking plasma-state reconstruction, actuator inference, and disruption warning from shared measurements to support more integrated, data-driven fusion plasma prediction and control research.

infographic.key_insight: GenToka uses one generative multimodal foundation model to connect plasma reconstruction, forecasting, actuator inference, and disruption warning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A shared model that adapts to different input-output schemas could reduce task-specific model development for tokamak prediction and control research.
method: Generate schema-selected targets jointly with a shared conditional diffusion Transformer.
Preserve time series, profiles, fields, and scalars through signal-specific codecs.
Transfer cross-signal structure through foundation pretraining and task-specific adaptation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 20 MAST tasks in six groups, GenToka reduced macro-average normalized RMSE versus TokaMind by 4.7% on Groups 1–4 and 17.7% on Group 5, and improved macro-average window-level F1 by 8.4% on Group 6 at a common validation-selected threshold.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation is reported on MAST measurements; transfer to other tokamaks and real-time control readiness remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: A Generative Foundation Model for Multimodal Tokamak Tasks

title: User Embeddings are Superpositions of Interpretable Behavioral Modes
authors: Jonathan Kozaczuk, Zheng Dong, Noyan Evirgen, Keivan Majidi, Eddie K. H. Ng, Chris Porter
abstract: User embeddings are central components of modern recommendation, personalization, and behavioral modeling systems. Though these embeddings can compactly encode rich behavioral information, they are inherently dense and opaque, limiting interpretability. To address this gap, we argue that user embeddings can be understood as sparse superpositions of interpretable behavioral modes. This structure is directly predicted by generative models of user behavior for linear embeddings and extends approximately to deep-learning representations by the superposition hypothesis. Superimposed modes can naturally be recovered by sparse dictionary learning methods, such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and recovered modes can be automatically named and queried in natural language. We validate mode recovery against known ground truth on synthetic data, where SAEs recover modes better than classical sparse baselines, including on transformer-encoded embeddings. We then apply the method to classical and transformer-based user embeddings from two real-world datasets. We also show how the corresponding natural-language labels enable zero-shot audience retrieval and characterization over embeddings never trained on text. The framework is post-hoc and model-agnostic, requiring no modification to the upstream embedding system.

infographic.key_insight: Dense user embeddings can be understood as sparse superpositions of interpretable behavioral modes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A post-hoc, model-agnostic interpretation layer can enable natural-language audience retrieval and characterization without changing the upstream embedding system.
method: Model user embeddings as sparse combinations of behavioral modes.
Recover modes using sparse dictionary learning, including sparse autoencoders.
Automatically name recovered modes and query them in natural language.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic ground-truth tests show better mode recovery with sparse autoencoders than classical sparse baselines, including for transformer-encoded embeddings; applications span two real-world datasets.
infographic.watch_item: The superposition account is approximate for deep representations, so recovered modes and their labels require validation before operational use.
infographic.paper_title: User Embeddings are Superpositions of Interpretable Behavioral Modes

title: Accelerating Safe Reinforcement Learning with Massive Parallelism
authors: Joonyoung Lim, Younghwan Yoo
abstract: We investigate the problem of scaling safe reinforcement learning (safe RL) to massively parallel training regimes, where a large number of environments are exe- cuted with short rollout horizons. Although this setting improves data throughput and wall-clock efficiency, it creates a mismatch with constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs), whose safety constraints are defined over full-episode cost returns. We address this mismatch by analyzing staggered environment resets as a phase-mixture distribution over short trajectory segments. This analysis charac- terizes the bias induced by phase coverage and motivates a phase-aggregated cost estimator that reconstructs episode-level cost estimates from short rollout batches. We further incorporate finite-sample uncertainty and distribution mismatch into a constraint-tightening framework, yielding a scalable Safe RL method compatible with on-policy optimization. Using an MJX-based implementation of Safety Gym, our experiments show that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to non-massively parallel implementations while substantially reducing wall-clock training time.

infographic.key_insight: Phase-aggregated cost estimation helps massively parallel safe reinforcement learning reconcile short training rollouts with full-episode safety constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables faster wall-clock training while retaining episode-level safety accounting in on-policy reinforcement learning.
method: Model staggered environment resets as a phase mixture of short trajectory segments.
Aggregate costs across phases to estimate full-episode costs.
Tighten constraints to account for finite-sample uncertainty and distribution mismatch.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments using an MJX-based Safety Gym implementation report performance comparable to non-massively parallel implementations with substantially reduced wall-clock training time.
infographic.watch_item: Uneven phase coverage can bias cost estimates, so deployment requires careful uncertainty and distribution-mismatch handling.
infographic.paper_title: Accelerating Safe Reinforcement Learning with Massive Parallelism

title: Learning a patient world model for health system simulation in intensive care
authors: Yingtai Li, Ruoyan Wang, Yu Li, Shaohua Kevin Zhou
abstract: Designing healthcare strategies requires anticipating their clinical and operational consequences before implementation, a task that often relies on health system simulation. Such a simulation necessitates modeling how patient states evolve and generate care demands. However, conventional approaches typically tailor compact state transitions to a single policy question and omit history-dependent dynamics, thus requiring the redefinition of states and transitions when there is a new question that entails different clinical information. We propose to learn a patient world model from longitudinal EHRs using a neural network to provide a shared clinical representation of patient trajectories that can serve simulation questions across scenarios. Taking ICU operations as an example, we train the model on MIMIC-IV, freeze it, and couple its time-queryable predictions to shared ICU calendars, resources, and queues via scenario-specific mappings, so that one model renders admission demand, care tasks, and discharge proposals across simulations evaluating ICU bed capacity, care dispatch, and post-ICU transfer capacity. Experiments show that our model matches Markov and semi-Markov comparators in aggregate occupancy and directional responses to capacity and dispatch policies. It also reproduces policy gains from replayed observed trajectories. For patients entering the same support state from different prior trajectories, the learned representation captures a 24-h recovery difference (-6.4 predicted versus -6.7 observed percentage points), a contrast missed by compact state models, which propagates into distinct simulated care demand, queue burden, and bed use. These results indicate that a learned world model of patient dynamics has the potential to replace question-specific state models, allowing new care policies to be evaluated by reconfiguring the scenario without model rebuilding.

infographic.key_insight: A learned patient world model can support multiple ICU policy simulations without rebuilding question-specific patient-state models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can reuse a frozen clinical model while reconfiguring ICU resources, queues, and scenario mappings to evaluate operational policies.
method: Train a neural patient-trajectory model on longitudinal MIMIC-IV EHRs.
Freeze the model and connect time-queryable predictions to shared ICU calendars, resources, and queues.
Use scenario-specific mappings to simulate bed capacity, care dispatch, and post-ICU transfer capacity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model matched Markov and semi-Markov comparators on aggregate occupancy and directional policy responses, reproduced replay-based policy gains, and captured a history-dependent 24-hour recovery contrast of −6.4 versus −6.7 observed percentage points.
infographic.watch_item: Simulation agreement does not establish real-world policy effects; deployment requires external validation and checks of scenario-mapping assumptions.
infographic.paper_title: Learning a patient world model for health system simulation in intensive care

title: Deep-learning surrogate model for rapid quantum-noise computation in dual-pump fiber-optic phase-sensitive amplifiers
authors: Yousra Bouasria, Debanuj Chatterjee, Abdessamad Belfakir, Debabrota Basu
abstract: Fiber-optic parametric amplifiers in a phase-sensitive amplifier (PSA) configuration are well known for their low noise properties. Quantum mechanics dictates that these amplifiers can have a 0 dB noise figure (NF) (ratio of signal-to-noise ratio at the input and output of the amplifier) under certain conditions. However, for a dual-pump configuration, when the system is highly nonlinear, fully quantum calculations of NF become non-trivial. In such cases, semi-quantum models of NF evaluation exists, however, they are often complicated and resource intensive. To simplify that, in this work, first we use a semi-quantum NF calculation framework for the generation of numerically simulated input-output dataset of NF over a large parameter spaces. Then we use the data to train an optimized deep neural network (DNN) for rapid NF prediction. Utilizing the DNN, we demonstrate about 400 times reduction in the computation time compared to the standard semi-quantum NF evaluation approach with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.0015 dB. Using clustering we demonstrate a rapid exploration of the parameter space with respect to high gain (20 dB) and low NF (0.3 dB) targets and retrieve associated design parameters. These results illustrate the efficacy of machine learning-based approaches for rapid search of high-dimensional parameter spaces especially in compute intensive photonic systems.

infographic.key_insight: A deep neural network predicts quantum noise figure in dual-pump fiber-optic phase-sensitive amplifiers about 400× faster than a semi-quantum calculation, with a mean absolute error of 0.0015 dB.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The surrogate enables rapid exploration of amplifier designs targeting 20 dB gain and 0.3 dB noise figure.
method: Generate simulated noise-figure data using a semi-quantum calculation framework.
Train an optimized deep neural network to predict noise figure from system parameters.
Use clustering to identify parameter regions associated with target gain and noise figure.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on numerically simulated data reports approximately 400× lower computation time and 0.0015 dB mean absolute error relative to the semi-quantum approach.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy is established against simulations; experimental validation and reliability outside the sampled parameter space are not reported in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Deep-learning surrogate model for rapid quantum-noise computation in dual-pump fiber-optic phase-sensitive amplifiers

title: Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement
authors: Wenbo Huang, Jianxin Bi, Shunyu Yang, Ruiyang Si, Rui Ni, Qiang Wang
abstract: Self-improving embodied agents are increasingly being developed and compared on robot simulation benchmarks. Several recent works expose the benchmark's success criteria to the learning agent, a practice we call Criteria Exposure (CE). These criteria, originally written to verify policies trained by imitation learning, often demand more than the corresponding language instructions, so a score from such a verifier may not faithfully reflect whether the instructed task was completed, especially for robot-control programs written by an agent. As embodied coding agents report ever higher benchmark scores, a natural question arises: when a coding agent is exposed to the benchmark's criteria, does it generate code that better performs the instructed task, or code that simply overfits to the verification criteria? We conduct controlled experiments with a self-improving agent with and without CE, and find that with CE the agent quickly produces code with a higher success rate under the given criteria, but this advantage disappears when the criteria are changed slightly without departing from the original instructions. More importantly, the skills the agent develops under CE transfer poorly across tasks. We further propose instruction-faithful criteria and show that they better reflect the performance of agent-generated programs.

infographic.key_insight: Exposing embodied coding agents to benchmark success criteria can improve verifier scores without improving instruction-faithful task performance or skill transfer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Robot-learning evaluations should test instruction-faithful task completion and cross-task transfer rather than rely solely on scores from exposed verifiers.
method: Compare a self-improving embodied agent with and without criteria exposure.
Reevaluate programs under slightly changed criteria that preserve the original instructions.
Assess cross-task skill transfer and propose instruction-faithful criteria.
infographic.evidence_signal: Controlled experiments show that criteria exposure quickly raises scores under the original verifier, but the advantage disappears after small instruction-consistent criteria changes, and learned skills transfer poorly.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report effect sizes or benchmark coverage, leaving the magnitude and generality of these findings uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement

title: Dynamic Optimistic Constrained OCO with Memory via Delay Equivalence
authors: Mohammed Abdullah, George Iosifidis, Salah Eddine Elayoubi, Tijani Chahed
abstract: Online Convex Optimization with memory and time-varying constraints (COCO-M) is a recently-introduced framework that captures the dynamics of stateful online learning and non-stochastic control with budget constraints. Despite its expressive power, COCO-M remains largely understudied. In this work, we tackle this problem in its full scale, providing an optimistic algorithm that incorporates untrusted predictions to tame universal dynamic regret and cumulative constraint violation. Our analysis leverages a potent reduction from memory to delay and treats state-dependent gradients as delayed feedback. We establish the first bounds that adapt to both environment non-stationarity (path length $P_T$) and prediction accuracy, while lifting previous restrictive assumptions such as functional separability. En route to these results, we derive findings of independent interest for the memory-to-delay reduction, and for delayed OCO with time-varying constraints. The proposed framework ensures sublinear worst-case guarantees that improve with prediction accuracy, reaching $\mathcal O(1)$ regret under perfect predictions, with cumulative constraint violation (CCV) $\mathcal O(\sqrt{T})$ for unknown $P_T$ and $\mathcal O(\log T)$ for known or online observable $P_T$ , while recovering the optimal COCO rates when memory disappears.

infographic.key_insight: Reducing memory to delayed feedback enables optimistic constrained online optimization with guarantees that adapt to environmental change and prediction accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports stateful online learning and non-stochastic control with time-varying constraints, using potentially unreliable forecasts to improve theoretical performance.
method: Reduce memory effects to delay by treating state-dependent gradients as delayed feedback.
Incorporate untrusted predictions into optimistic constrained online optimization.
Adapt bounds to comparator path length and prediction accuracy without assuming functional separability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical guarantees, not empirical evaluation: perfect predictions yield O(1) regret, with cumulative constraint violation O(√T) for unknown path length or O(log T) when it is known or online observable.
infographic.watch_item: Stronger constraint-violation guarantees require known or online-observable path length; practical runtime and empirical robustness are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamic Optimistic Constrained OCO with Memory via Delay Equivalence

title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts
authors: Yubo Wang, Rui Meng, Jaehyun Nam, Tomas Pfister, Jinsung Yoon
abstract: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.

infographic.key_insight: Preserving recovered execution procedures in reusable artifacts raises ML reproduction success while reducing downstream API spending.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Packaging code, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide can make research handoffs more reliable across coding agents.
method: ReproBridge constructs standardized, refined artifacts from research code and recovered procedures.
Agents attempt reproduction in fresh sessions using raw code or refined artifacts.
A separate Auditor checks execution evidence.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four models on ReproBridge-Bench's 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, refined artifacts increased mean success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduced downstream API spending by 19.7% on average.
infographic.watch_item: Reported downstream API savings do not establish whether they offset the upfront cost of constructing and validating refined artifacts.
infographic.paper_title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts

title: Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks
authors: E. Kelly Buchanan, Crystal Zhou, Scott W. Linderman, Christopher Ré
abstract: Coding agents are among the most economically consequential deployments of LLMs to date, making reliable evaluation increasingly important. Yet even benchmarks that are carefully validated at release can become stale. As models improve, they can discover valid solutions that existing verifiers reject, while changes to evaluation infrastructure can invalidate assumptions embedded in tasks and tests. We call the resulting accumulation of defects benchmark maintenance debt: a growing gap between benchmark scores and the capabilities they are intended to measure. We introduce a continuous-validation workflow for agentic benchmarks that combines community reports, task artifacts, agent traces, automated oracle checks, and human-gated repairs. We apply this workflow to Terminal-Bench 2.0, a benchmark that underwent extensive human and LM-assisted review and red-teaming before release. Our audit identifies issues in roughly 30% of the benchmark, and we release the resulting repairs as Terminal-Bench 2.1. These repairs change evaluation results: accuracy increased by over 10 percentage points and leaderboard positions move by up to three ranks, even as the overall ranking remains highly correlated (Spearman rho = 0.958). We evaluate how resource allocation shapes benchmark conclusions. We show that fixed wall-clock can materially change agent performance: For example, extending the time limit closes a 20pp harness gap on GPT 5.4 and shrinks a 30 pp gap on GPT 5.4 mini to 5 pp. Benchmark maintenance is therefore not only about repairing task artifacts: resource budgets are part of the measurement specification and must be validated alongside the tasks themselves. More broadly, benchmark maintenance debt is not just accumulated implementation bugs: our results show that as models improve, both evaluation assumptions and resource settings may need to be revalidated.

infographic.key_insight: Benchmarks accumulate maintenance debt as agents and infrastructure evolve, so reliable evaluation requires continuous validation of both tasks and resource budgets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Treat agent benchmarks as maintained software: version repairs, audit verifiers, and validate time limits before interpreting scores or rankings.
method: Combine community reports, task artifacts, agent traces, and automated oracle checks.
Apply human-gated repairs to Terminal-Bench 2.0 and release Terminal-Bench 2.1.
Compare evaluation results and test how time budgets affect harness performance gaps.
infographic.evidence_signal: The audit found issues in roughly 30% of tasks; repairs increased accuracy by over 10 percentage points and shifted leaderboard positions by up to three ranks, while rankings remained strongly correlated (Spearman ρ = 0.958).
infographic.watch_item: Repairs alone do not ensure comparable results: extending time limits closed or substantially reduced reported harness gaps, making resource settings part of the measurement specification.
infographic.paper_title: Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks

title: StrataFlux: Memory-Hierarchy-Native Low-Bit LLM Inference
authors: Jake Hyun, Ziyu Zhao, Jae-sun Seo, Mohamed S. Abdelfattah
abstract: Quantization reduces the memory and bandwidth demands of large language model (LLM) inference but can degrade accuracy; offloading higher-precision data can instead stall generation. We introduce StrataFlux, a framework that challenges this tradeoff by recovering accuracy lost to low-bit weight and key-value (KV) cache quantization while retaining quantization's memory and speed advantages. StrataFlux co-designs refinement representation, selection, and delivery to make host RAM and solid-state drives useful sources of additional precision. Its selective precision streaming reduces transfer volume, overlaps delivery with computation, and reuses fetched precision across decoding steps so generation need not wait for every transfer. We evaluate 2-4-bit weights and 2-3-bit KV-cache on dedicated GPUs and unified-memory platforms. For 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, StrataFlux reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while maintaining 95.4% of the quantized base's throughput on RTX 5090. With 2-bit weights and KV, StrataFlux raises Qwen3-8B's AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use. At 128K context, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 3-bit weights and 2-bit KV achieves comparable perplexity and speed to vLLM's 4-bit AWQ weights and 8-bit KV on RTX 5090, using approximately half the GPU memory. These results show that GPU-resident precision need not set the accuracy ceiling, nor offloading-tier latency dictate decoding speed.

infographic.key_insight: StrataFlux selectively streams extra precision from host RAM and SSDs to recover low-bit LLM accuracy while largely preserving quantization’s memory and speed benefits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Memory-hierarchy-aware inference can support accurate models and long contexts with less GPU memory, without requiring all precision data to remain GPU-resident.
method: Co-design refinement representation, selection, and delivery for low-bit weights and KV caches.
Selectively stream additional precision from host RAM and SSDs.
Overlap transfers with computation and reuse fetched precision across decoding steps.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across dedicated-GPU and unified-memory evaluations, StrataFlux reduced 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 at 95.4% of base throughput on RTX 5090 and raised Qwen3-8B AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits may depend on host-memory and SSD bandwidth, transfer scheduling, and how effectively fetched precision can be reused.
infographic.paper_title: StrataFlux: Memory-Hierarchy-Native Low-Bit LLM Inference

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Heterogeneous Cognitive and Biomedical Knowledge Graphs: The Role of Graph Grounding in Multi-Hop Reasoning and Hallucination Mitigation
authors: Ali Sarabadani, Kheirolah Rahsepar Fard, Tahereh Jeirani
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in biomedical and cognitive neuroscience, but their ability to reason reliably over heterogeneous knowledge graphs (KGs) remains unclear. We benchmark five LLMs (GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.0 Pro, Llama 3, Qwen, and BioGPT) across five KGs: DrugBank, NeuroSynth, Cognitive Atlas, Brain Map, and GDPKG. We introduce a multitier query dataset to evaluate reasoning depth and factual accuracy under KG-aware (graph-grounded) and KG-agnostic conditions. Inter-annotator agreement was substantial, with Cohen's kappa of 0.781 (range: 0.753-0.807) and Fleiss' kappa of 0.77. Results show that general-purpose models, particularly GPT-5.1 and Gemini 2.0 Pro, generally outperform domain-specific models on multi-hop and high-level reasoning tasks, although performance declines as query complexity increases. KG grounding reduces hallucination rates across all evaluated models. Contrary to our initial hypothesis, domain-specific models do not consistently outperform general-purpose models on specialized tasks without graph grounding. These findings highlight the value of combining broad language-model capabilities with structured domain knowledge. We provide practical guidance for selecting LLM-KG integration strategies based on task complexity and computational constraints, and discuss hybrid neurosymbolic architectures for personalized medicine, cognitive disorder diagnosis, and explainable AI.

infographic.key_insight: Graph grounding reduces hallucinations across evaluated LLMs, while general-purpose models generally lead on multi-hop and high-level reasoning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Pair broad-capability LLMs with structured domain knowledge, selecting integration strategies according to reasoning complexity and computational constraints.
method: Benchmark five LLMs: GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.0 Pro, Llama 3, Qwen, and BioGPT.
Evaluate across DrugBank, NeuroSynth, Cognitive Atlas, Brain Map, and GDPKG.
Compare graph-grounded and graph-agnostic conditions using multitier queries.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark reports substantial annotation agreement (Cohen’s κ = 0.781; Fleiss’ κ = 0.77), declining performance with query complexity, and reduced hallucinations with graph grounding.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no effect sizes or runtime costs, limiting assessment of grounding’s practical accuracy–compute trade-off.
infographic.paper_title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Heterogeneous Cognitive and Biomedical Knowledge Graphs: The Role of Graph Grounding in Multi-Hop Reasoning and Hallucination Mitigation
